source.title: MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong recent preprint with released code, explicit train/validation/evaluation protocol, a structured six-dimensional harness space, a dual-layer experience bank, held-out case adaptation without test-time labels, three source benchmark families, six external evaluation suites, and six additional base models. The paper explicitly leaves statistical robustness and fine-grained component attribution to future work.
assessments.quantitative_result: The final validation-selected harness improves over base on all three reported source benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 0.722→0.806, LiveCodeBench 0.900→0.967, and FinanceAgent 0.600→0.767. Cross-model Terminal-Bench transfer improves all six additional tested models, with mean gain +0.098 and range +0.038 (GPT-4.1) to +0.233 (GLM-5). Cross-dataset transfer is selective: the Terminal-Bench-derived harness improves MMMLU +0.030, StrongReject +0.030 and SWE-Bench Pro +0.059, while saturated suites do not move and LawBench is mixed. On the 18-task Terminal-Bench held-out split MemoHarness uses 14.18M input tokens, 13.32M cached, and reports $6.89 cost versus $10.28 for Codex and $9.51 for Claude Code under its price/caching accounting. Operation-level adjacent-transition analysis reports large associations for some added operations such as cat (8/11 positive, 72.7%, +59.5pp over the transition baseline), but the paper labels these associations rather than causal ablations.
assessments.matched_baseline: Moderate-to-good. Source-benchmark final harnesses are compared against fixed/released baseline harnesses and validation-selected rather than test-peak checkpoints. Cross-dataset comparisons use the same GPT-5.3-Codex base. However, product-specific baselines are not pure scaffold-only ablations, the full adaptive harness changes several dimensions jointly, and per-operation analyses are observational adjacent-transition associations.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Moderate for the bundled claim that execution experience can optimize and selectively adapt an agent harness. Weak for attributing gains to any one of context/tool/orchestration/memory/output dimensions or to the dual-layer bank specifically. The source itself explicitly says finer component attribution is needed.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Good: public code and full arXiv HTML expose protocol, benchmark splits, costs, transfer tables and implementation details. This comparator directly verified the primary HTML metrics.
assessments.failure_evidence: Useful negative evidence against universal harness transfer: external-suite gains are selective, saturated tasks do not move, LawBench is mixed, and high-level operation/reward associations are not causal evidence.
scope_limits: Recent preprint under review; no independent replication or significance analysis establishing robust population-level effects.
Primary Terminal-Bench held-out set is only 18 tasks under the reported protocol.
Full-harness search is composite; component causality is unresolved.
Cross-model transfer uses the same learned harness and is encouraging but remains one task family.
Cost advantage depends materially on caching assumptions and public price accounting.
Operation-level positive-transition rates should not be treated as intervention-effect estimates.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B for MemoHarness as a bundled adaptive harness optimization/test-time adaptation system with useful cross-model and selective cross-dataset transfer.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- at most until any O-facing control-layer adaptation is decomposed into matched interventions and evaluated on held-out tasks/models with component attribution, cost, and regression controls.

source.title: Group-Evolving Agents: Open-Ended Self-Improvement via Experience Sharing

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong primary self-evolution study with public code, two difficult coding benchmarks, a directly compared DGM self-evolving baseline under the same number of evolved agents, cross-coding-model transfer/robustness analysis, and lineage-functionality analysis. It remains a composite preprint method and no independent external replication was identified.
assessments.quantitative_result: Under the reported matched number of evolved agents, GEA reaches 71.0% versus DGM 56.7% on SWE-bench Verified and 88.3% versus 68.3% on Polyglot. It reports framework-level bug repair in 1.4 iterations on average versus 5 for the compared self-evolving method. The best GEA agent integrates 8 of 9 key functionalities versus 5 for the best DGM agent and incorporates experience from 17 unique ancestors versus 9 for DGM, supporting the interpretation that discoveries from multiple evolutionary branches are being consolidated rather than remaining isolated.
assessments.matched_baseline: Good at the system level: GEA and DGM are compared under the same number of evolved agents on the same coding benchmarks. The comparison does not independently randomize group selection, performance-novelty selection, experience pooling, consolidation policy, or other architecture changes, so it is not a clean isolated ablation of cross-lineage sharing alone.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Moderately strong for group-level evolution as a bundled mechanism and for the association between cross-ancestor consolidation and stronger late-stage performance. Only moderate/weak for the narrower claim that experience sharing itself, independent of group selection and consolidation design, causes the full gain.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Good: official public code is linked and the primary arXiv abstract directly verifies the headline matched-budget benchmark gains and bug-repair result. Component-level reproduction was not performed here.
assessments.failure_evidence: Directly demonstrates that tree-structured isolated self-evolution can underutilize exploratory diversity under this coding substrate; however, it does not prove every isolated-lineage architecture is inferior or that unrestricted sharing is safe.
scope_limits: Coding-agent domain and a DGM-derived evolutionary substrate.
Composite group-evolution method rather than isolated experience-sharing treatment.
Shared experience can also propagate bad changes; provenance/transfer validation is not established by the headline comparison alone.
Benchmark gains should not be generalized to open-ended scientific research or O without matched transfer tests.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for GEA's composite group-evolution system under matched evolved-agent budgets on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C for cross-lineage lesson transfer in O/external research until a direct isolated-vs-shared-lineage experiment measures both useful transfer and harmful-propagation rates with provenance.

source.title: Scaling Self-Evolving Agents via Parametric Memory

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong current primary preprint with two Qwen3 model scales, conversational-memory, multi-objective search and filtered continual-learning evaluations, summary/retrieval memory baselines, post-RL matched-protocol comparisons, three-run averaged results, explicit time/GPU-memory accounting, and four targeted fast-weight component ablations. It is not peer reviewed in this pass and no independent replication was located.
assessments.quantitative_result: Before RL, TMEM exceeds the strongest explicit-memory baseline on LongMemEval-S by +4.79 F1/+2.34 EM with Qwen3-4B and +10.21/+7.02 with Qwen3-8B; search gains for Qwen3-4B are +1.92/+1.13 on four objectives and +1.86/+1.16 on eight objectives, while the Qwen3-8B four-objective gain is only +1.00/+0.23 and explicitly treated as directional. After matched RL, TMEM gets the largest absolute conversational gains (+5.12 F1/+5.02 EM on LoCoMo; +4.92/+4.84 on LongMemEval-S) and exceeds the strongest explicit-memory baseline after RL by +4.34/+3.29 on four-objective search and +4.36/+2.63 on eight-objective search. Component ablations are substantial: SVD initialization improves LongMemEval-S 38.54/22.33→41.24/25.54; grounded QA supervision beats free-form summary 35.44/20.18→41.24/25.54 and raw next-token 10.37/7.62; training both LoRA factors instead of freezing the SVD projection adds only +0.27 F1/+0.12 EM on LongMemEval-S. Context-trigger budget is bell-shaped, with dataset-specific optima such as 4096 for LoCoMo and 12288 for LongMemEval-S.
assessments.matched_baseline: Strong for a preprint. Summary/retrieval/no-memory strategies are compared in the same local evaluation pipeline, post-RL training data/task formats/rollout budgets/update schedules are held aligned across memory strategies, and several TMEM internals are ablated one at a time. Architectural differences between explicit and parametric memory mean the comparison necessarily includes different compute/memory profiles.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for several internal components and moderately strong for the overall fast-parametric-memory mechanism on the tested memory-centric/search tasks. Online LoRA adaptation and explicit memory compression are bundled in TMEM, but supervision form, subspace initialization, update-mode and trigger budget are separately tested.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Primary arXiv HTML directly exposes tables, three-run averages, ablations and efficiency accounting. No official code or independent reproduction was confirmed by this comparator in this pass.
assessments.failure_evidence: Important non-monotonic evidence: overly frequent memory compression loses detail, overly large context degrades extraction quality, a smaller-model/multi-objective setting shows only directional gain, and supervision format materially changes memory quality. This argues against treating 'move experience into weights' as automatically useful regardless of extraction/trigger design.
scope_limits: Preprint with Qwen3-4B/8B rather than frontier-scale foundation models.
Memory-centric benchmarks and filtered CL-Bench answerable subset; not a broad autonomous-agent capability evaluation.

Online parameter updates add GPU/optimization complexity: TMEM uses 21.3GB/22.9GB in the paper's Qwen3-4B LoCoMo/LongMemEval-S accounting versus lower memory for summary/retrieval baselines, though latency is competitive in some settings.
Parametric writes can create harder-to-audit persistence and forgetting/contamination risks not fully characterized by the reported benchmarks.
No evidence supports modifying O's primary foundation-model weights; any transfer should begin in an isolated adapter/proxy setting.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for TMEM's fast-LoRA parametric memory mechanism and its tested component choices across the reported Qwen3 memory/search benchmarks.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C at most for O until an isolated, reversible fast-adapter experiment beats bounded explicit memory on matched downstream outcomes while quantifying compute, auditability, negative transfer and recovery.

cross_source_synthesis: The three self-improvement candidates operate at different adaptation layers: MemoHarness changes the external control layer, GEA changes the evolutionary population and experience-transfer structure, and TMEM changes a fast parametric memory substrate. Their evidence should not be collapsed into a generic 'self-improvement works' claim.

MemoHarness has useful transfer evidence but weaker component causality; GEA has strong matched system-level gains but cannot isolate experience sharing from the composite group-evolution method; TMEM has the best component ablation depth of the three but is limited to smaller models and memory-centric tasks.

All three show scope/non-monotonicity constraints: selective MemoHarness transfer, unisolated GEA component effects and a directional TMEM setting/bell-shaped trigger budget. These are reasons for matched mechanism-level tests, not family-level rejection.
